utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, as I said, we will sit this afternoon until sometime after half past four. Have you made some arrangements for the witness to come back?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite, Mr. President. We have agreed with the witness that the 25th of November, in the morning, would be the date which would be quite convenient for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Duncan, yesterday you finished testifying about the missile which was fired at your camp and the results of the investigation which Colonel Blaskic talked about. Less than a week after that fire, your interpreter, Ms. Dobrila Kolaba, was killed; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It happened on the 5th of July, 1993; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you get the results under which this shot was fired by an isolated soldier of the HVO, which resulted in the death of your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my opinion, yes. That was my opinion of the events at the time and the responsibility for the person who did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your opinion and the angle from which the shot was fired, you established that that shot was fired from a position which was held by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: May I just object at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, this is in issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is in issue. Also, it's not charged in the amended indictment. We've heard a lot of evidence about this already from the person who actually conducted the investigation into this incident. I would submit that it's not relevant. Similarly, there are two other subjects which fall into the same category: the shooting of the UNHCR driver, about which the Trial Chamber has already heard a lot of evidence, and also the assault on Grbavica on September the 8th, once again about which the Trial Chamber has heard a lot of evidence. None of these things are charged in the amended indictment, and we would respectfully submit that they are irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may be, but if they are in dispute, the Prosecution are entitled to adduce evidence about it. But, Mr. Lopez-Terres, you can do that fairly briefly because we have heard evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What explanations were you given by Colonel Blaskic regarding the person who fired the shot, about the person who was responsible for it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a number of explanations as to a possibility, that it could be a Muslim who had moved across from his side of the front lines to the south, occupied the house temporarily, and shot the interpreter from there. It was judged to be by a person or persons unknown, who had then moved back, as it were, to his own lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreter that we are talking about was not a Muslim, was she?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she was not. She was Serbian by origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you voice some hypothesis regarding the reasons for which that particular shot was fired?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were two reasons the shot was fired to kill her: Firstly, because she had accompanied Bob Stewart for most of his six-month tour and, therefore, had been a party to many of the conferences he had been to with both Croat and Muslim forces; secondly, I think it was done deliberately to upset me as a new commander in post, as a way of perhaps expressing their resentment of some of my actions in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 5th of July, at the time when Dobrila Kolaba was killed, were there other people in the camp who were fired at?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just the one shot was fired. She was shot in the head and she died before she hit the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The explanation which was given you that a Muslim might have fired that shot, did that sound plausible to you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't sound at all plausible, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little bit later, on the 14th of July, 1993, the driver of the UNHCR was killed as he was driving his vehicle in Stari Vitez; do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think, if I recall it, his name was Boris; he was driving an armoured UNHCR vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, you mentioned the date of the 14th of July. I notice that the summary refers to the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 14th of August. If I said the 14th of July, then it was merely a slip of the tongue. The 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's understandable in your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We would stipulate, Your Honours, that it was the 14th of August of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the 14th of August; there is no question about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what explanation were you given regarding the origin of fire of the shot which killed that driver?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation I was given by the HVO forces was that this shot had again been fired by person or persons unknown, possibly a Muslim, deliberately at the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That explanation, did that sound plausible to you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That explanation did not sound plausible, on the basis that the UNHCR were trying, as I was, to get aid into the Stari Vitez area, the pocket of Muslims who were there. It is, therefore, unlikely that a Muslim would have fired that shot, and, indeed, as far as I was concerned, the shot had come from the direction of the HVO lines around Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little bit later, but during the same period of time, you were notified about proper orchestration of a thing by the HVO soldiers who were loading ammunition into a vehicle belonging to the UNHCR, and it was the HVO soldiers who spoke about that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was my understanding that soldiers from my battalion had been stopped and blocked whilst escorting a convoy, and at that stage HVO soldiers had loaded ammunitions onto one of the trucks. They then moved away from those vehicles, started filming, and recorded the miraculous find of arms and weapons on an UNHCR vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this whole performance?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was to make a propaganda film, which they had obviously made to show to their people that they couldn't trust both the U.N. and UNHCR, who were clearly running, in their opinion, running weapons and supplies through to Muslim forces in their area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of August 1993, and notably on the 19th of August, 1993, you had an opportunity of talking to Colonel Blaskic, who voiced certain threats, saying that he would blow up the ammunitions factory in Vitez if Vitez was taken over by the Muslims; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so. Commander Tihomir Blaskic briefed me in some detail as to the results of an explosion in the factory, saying that it contained poisonous gases and liquids, and that the result would be almost probably the destruction of the entire Lasva Valley, an area some 60 kilometres by 100 kilometres long, which would be affected for some time. It would be a huge explosion, resulting in a massive loss of life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take this threat as a form of blackmail?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took it as a direct threat against both my own forces and UNHCR. And it was being held, therefore -- he was intending to hold me responsible should he have to blow things up. And therefore I did regard it quite clearly as a blackmailing threat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Duncan, I should like to show you a report of your regiment of the 17th of August, which is Z1172, of the 17th of August. Will you please look at passage 4 on the document and tell us if this report bears on the threat that you have just told us about?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It refers to it, that Blaskic mentioned he had a considerable amount of explosive and available in the factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And saying that he had 100 kilograms of explosives for every Muslim soldier, was that the wording that was used by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes. It's to certainly amplify, make entirely clear the amount of explosives he had in the factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 4th of September, 1993, Colonel Blaskic came to the camp of your regiment and conveyed to you a message from Dario Kordic. Do you remember that message?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 4th of September. He came to my camp and we talked about a number of matters, the matters we always talked of. But the prime purpose of his visit on the 4th of September was to give me a message from Dario Kordic, that there would be no more exchanges of wounded out of the Vitez pocket. This exchange of wounded had been by mutual agreement between the BiH and the HVO, but the message from Kordic relayed by Blaskic was that all arrangements were now finished, and there would be no agreement of the evacuation of any more of the HVO or the BiH out of combat areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about the wounded, were there also civilians amongst them, or only military wounded?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were in the hospital at times children, women, people with mental problems, and people with both wounds from the war and serious illnesses, such as cancer. None were to be moved from then onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were two categories of wounded there to be covered by this exchange; it was two categories of wounded?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, it was all wounded. There was no differentiation at all. I had been personally around that hospital and seen all those wounded people, and so I was well aware that there were women and children and other people in that hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that message which was brought to you by Colonel Blaskic from Dario Kordic, in what form was it done? Was it merely verbally or was it in writing?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in writing. It was a written message.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Colonel Blaskic read that message out to you, did he?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. He read the message out to me. I do not have and was not given a copy of the message.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the following days, you left the area of Vitez, and it was during that period of time that Grbavica was attacked. I am not asking you about the details of that attack, just a comment regarding the nature of destruction inflicted on the area of Grbavica during that attack.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Grbavica took place two days after I had left for two weeks' military leave as part of my seven-month, eight-month tour in Central Bosnia. The attack involved the massive destruction of property on the top of that hill where the Grbavica was based, in my opinion, totally above and beyond what was required to secure that hill by military means. I had no problem with the concept of that hill being secured. It was a clear military objective. But I believe the way in which it was secured showed excessive use of violence against the local population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also observe that in other villages which you visited?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times, yes, there was also destruction on other villages. The level of destruction would normally result in -- as a result of prolonged battles over an area which had become fixed and static front line, because both sides will be shelling each other or mortaring each other for some time. But in this case what was significant about Grbavica was the level of destruction done in such a short time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as regards other villages that you saw the large-scale destruction, was it always justified by military objectives?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time how did you interpret the justification, the explanation of that scale of destruction?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the destruction was done to ensure that no one who ever lived or had lived in that village could ever return, because of the wholesale destruction. It would have required a complete rebuild of the area to get it back to anything -- like, it was a complete flattening and raising, if you like, of the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You therefore confirmed that on the 22nd of September, 1993 you talked to the liaison officer, Colonel Blaskic, called Darko Gelic [Realtime transcript read in error "Kraljevic"] regarding the threats to two officers that we spoke about yesterday, that is, Lee Whitworth and Mark Bower, in relation to that attack?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came to tell me, not for the first time, that my two liaison officers, Bower and Whitworth, were being threatened by HVO forces. The normal wording was along the lines of we could no longer -- we, the HVO, could no longer guarantee their security as they move around and about. My reply was the normal reply, which was this was totally unacceptable, on the basis that I had threats, similar threats issued against myself, that no one could -- no one would be responsible should HVO soldiers decide to have a go, as it were, at me and my officers. It's irritating and I thought a rather foolish way of doing business. I should perhaps add that my normal response for such threats was to drive straight down to the Hotel Vitez and speak with Colonel Blaskic about them, firstly, because it embarrassed him enormously, but it also normally sorted out the problem as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a detail for the transcript. It says Darko Kraljevic is the name of the liaison officer. Evidently, that is not Darko Kraljevic, but Darko Gelic. On the 27th of September, 1993, General, you again went to the cottage, to the summer cottage that you spoke about yesterday, to talk to Dario Kordic about the problem, about a certain problem, that is, the blockade of Stari Vitez. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The purpose of the meeting was, firstly, to take my successor, who is a Lieutenant-Colonel Peter Williams, to meet Dario Kordic. And secondly, as of that moment I believed that Tihomir Blaskic was away and not in the Vitez pocket. I wanted to discuss some matters between us. Those matters were to do with freedom of movement, which he assured me personally that we now had freedom of movement throughout the area; that is, freedom of movement for U.N. vehicles and UNHCR vehicles. But that he did confirm most strongly that further access to the pocket of Stari Vitez would be denied for as long as the forces of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, the BiH, continued attacking the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that announced by the person responsible for civilian affairs in your camp? And I believe it was two days after your discussion with Dario Kordic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was issued two days before my discussion, and that's the reason I went to speak to Dario Kordic about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to show you a document, which seems to be related to what we're talking about. It is the document 1213, and it was already produced during the testimony of another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at the penultimate paragraph and tell us whether it refers to that discussion about the U.N. civilian officer.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that confirms what I just said. This was two days before, where my civil defence officer, Mr. Randy Rhodes, who is a citizen of the United States, who worked for some months with me in the British Battalion area, had met with Dario Kordic, as it says, and the denial of access to Stari Vitez was going to continue until the BiH ceased their current attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During October 1993, another humanitarian aid convoy was to pass through your area of responsibility, and you decided at that time, I believe, to reroute this convoy, to make it take another route rather than the one which had been envisaged.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This, I believe, was in the middle of October, round about the 16th or 17th. I should make it clear: This convoy was not a U.N. or UNHCR convoy; it was a convoy similar to the previous Muslim convoy that wished to come up through the Vitez pocket and on to the north, to the Tuzla area. I had decided that it would be foolish to again risk this convoy coming through the Vitez pocket, and therefore I made arrangements for it to move round through the Travnik area, and those arrangements were made with the BiH. It would move off to the west, around to the Travnik area. I did not tell the HVO commanders about these arrangements that I'd made to divert the convoy, in the event the convoy was diverted and got through successfully, but at the same time, my liaison officers reported to me that there were a number of HVO soldiers which had formed an ambush position on the entry point to the Vitez pocket, which was the road that ran from Gornji Vakuf up through. The only people that were aware of this convoy coming were myself and the senior commanders, who were aware of the convoy's arrival -- that is, the senior HVO commanders, who were aware of the convoy's arrival; timings, roughly, but no details of routes. The assumption was that we were going to use the same route as we'd used last time; that's up from Gornji Vakuf, Novi Travnik, through Vitez, and then up and away to Zenica. I should add that I spoke briefly, in a heated discussion, with Tihomir Blaskic after the convoy had been rerouted. When he asked me why I had not sent it along the valley, as he assumed it would go along that way, I replied, fairly bluntly, words to the effect that his track record stank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To go a little bit ^back?, concerning your meeting with Dario Kordic in Busovaca on the 27th of September, do you perhaps recall, how did Dario Kordic behave that day? What was his conduct? Was he in a particular mood? Did you notice anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly. He was in a fairly cheerful mood, I think, at that stage. He was very pleased to be introduced to my successor, which I had done out of politeness. But he seemed entirely happy to take decisions and front up, as it were, for these important decisions regarding freedom of movement and blocking the route into Stari Vitez. Very calm, very much in command, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he perhaps explain why he was assuring you that the convoy could move freely, whilst two days before that, he said something completely different to Randy Rhodes?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. He obviously had a change of heart and realised that if we blocked all convoys, then no aid would get through to his own people either; therefore, he was, if you like, cutting off his nose to spite his face, and it would be better to allow all convoys through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back now to the second Convoy of Joy that you already told us. On the 16th or 17th of October, you told us that there were soldiers setting up a kind of an ambush on the route which the convoy was supposed to take. Do you know where, and how did you learn that it was Zarko Andric, nicknamed Zuti, who was there awaiting the convoy?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned this from my liaison officers, who, you will remember, are a team that worked very closely for me, reporting back directly, and my liaison officer from that area reported that it was Zuti. I do not know his other name and I have never met Zuti, save that he was reported as the commander of the troops that had formed that ambush, and the ambush was facing across the road on the way that these trucks would obviously have to come up, should they come up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What reputation did Zuti enjoy? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a black marketeer, I believe. He was racketeering. He was using the war for his own personal ends. He had, on occasion, it was reported to me, met Muslims at the interface between the two forces, the HVO and the BiH, outside my camp in Vitez. Not a very rosy picture. Responsible for hijacking vehicles and running a gangster organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a former policeman, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes. He was a former policeman, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever met this gentleman, Zarko Andric?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Duncan, I should now like to show you, because we're talking about that individual, to show you briefly some comments which this person made to a journal, Globus. This was an interview, and there he made some comments about you. This is document 2784.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I'm going to object to this. Apparently, it's a newspaper article published after the beginning of this case, in Globus, which I believe is a Croatian newspaper. It concerns interviews and hearsay upon hearsay upon hearsay. It has no reliability whatsoever, and I don't think that it's helpful to the Trial Chamber in addressing issues that occurred in 1992 and 1994 when it was published last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It makes scurrilous allegations against the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't rely on those allegations, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lopez-Terres, does it take us any further?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wanted the Chamber to hear which were these comments, the observations which are made on his account by this man, Zuti, and the witness just told us that he had never met that person. It merely shows the credibility of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Zuti is not a witness. We've heard some other evidence about him, I think. I don't think it's going to take us any further to read about his sort of comments here. As I say, they're scurrilous and nobody is going to rely on them. So I don't think we're assisted by that. If you would like to move on now and let's see if we can finish this examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To conclude, that person accused General Duncan of very serious crimes, and I merely wanted to hear what General Duncan would want to tell us as regards these allegations; nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, General Duncan, during your activities there, while you were in command in that region, did you have an opportunity to personally note the presence of soldiers, of the troops of the Republic of Croatia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of reports from my soldiers who regularly passed along the road which we'd cut from an area south of Gornji Vakuf, right down to the south, to Tomislavgrad, of HV soldiers moving on that route, not frequently but from time to time. Although I can't remember the date exactly, I can remember returning from Tomislavgrad on one particular day and seeing a D-32 howitzer, a truck with HV markings, and, as I remember it, two soldiers with HV flashes on their shoulders. This artillery was used, I believe, to engage the Muslim forces in the Gornji Vakuf area, and the sightings were below the lakes -- I saw them below the lakes in the Prozor area. I only personally saw them once, but I did have reports from my subordinates. In addition, it was a standard task for anyone moving between Vitez and the south to watch out for anything they saw -- civilians, HVO, HV, or any military activity -- along the routes they travelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question. You already spoke about this yesterday. Could you indicate to the Court, could you tell the Court about the conclusions that you arrived at at the end of your term in that area regarding the authority of the HDZ political authorities and the HVO authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I object to that as beyond the stated expertise -- the military expertise of this witness, Mr. President. I believe he has already given several opinions in this vein, and I think that any such opinions would simply be speculation and surmise on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wanted to hear the conclusions that the witness arrived at. This is a witness who is fully entitled to arrive at some conclusions, whatever their worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit the evidence on this basis, that the witness was present and observing and, therefore, was in a position to form a view about these matters, but we will be grateful if it could be dealt with briefly.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, thank you. I will be brief, as directed. I think during the time I was there, I could sum events up by saying that a couple days after my arrival, I was visited by the senior or one of the senior HDZ officers, that is, Valenta, and briefed in detail, and I have already explained that briefing, what it covers, and therefore there's no point in repeating it, save to say that I thought he had expounded the feelings -- the political will of the HVO in that area and the HDZ in that area. After that I saw a number of events that I believe put that well into effect, and, if you like, Ahmici was the trigger before my arrival, in that this hatred of the Muslims and a requirement to clear them away, assisted by the JNA, as expounded by Valenta, was put into effect by the team of three people: that is, Valenta, with the doctrine and concepts; Kordic, who had the political control of the people; and Tihomir Blaskic, who actually owned most of the forces, the instrument. And during my time there, those three elements combined the team. I noted that Kordic had considerable influence and power, and we have already recorded and talked about those occasions where he was able to take swift, decisive action in the area and also laid down policy within the Vitez pocket. In summary, then, the team was working together to an organised programme with a clear aim. I also noted it was unusual for politicians to be so closely allied to the military; to have an office in a military headquarters and to be based in there is, in my experience, very unusual. There was clearly a tight control over the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers. Cross-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Brigadier. Sir, my name is Steve Sayers. Together with my colleague, Mitko Naumovski, we represent Dario Kordic. These gentlemen to my right, Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Mikulicic, they represent the other accused, Mario Cerkez. Now, General, or Brigadier, rather, you are not contending, I believe, that Mr. Kordic controlled the military police, are you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would contend that Mr. Kordic controlled the military police as and when it was required, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You actually do draw a distinction between the civilian police and the military police, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They are two different entities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you remember covering precisely that point in the Blaskic case about one and a half years ago, and expressing the opinion that while it was your view that Mr. Kordic had some influence over the local police, you stressed that he had no influence over the military police?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, I made that statement to a Mr. Hayman, who was investigating and defending the Tihomir Blaskic. And I made that statement, I think, in April 1996, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the light -- at that stage I had not reflected on any events between 1993, when I left Central Bosnia, and that time. Since then I have had time to look at my diaries and reflect more on events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's take a look at the statement that you made to the Prosecutors, including Mr. Gregory Kehoe. I take it you remember meeting with him in December of 1996?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were interviewed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please make a pause between question and answer, for the sake of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you are being asked to observe a pause between question and answer, and the same goes for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, I'll slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Also, I think if you are going to cross-examine the witness about his statement in detail, he should have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I agree entirely, Mr. President, and we have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder if you would turn to page 3. And the large paragraph in the page actually describes the Convoy of Joy incident upon which --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could one copy, please, be placed on the ELMO, because the interpreters do not have this statement. Could it be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just been interrupted by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could a copy be placed on the ELMO, because the interpreters do not have copies of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if we could put a copy of this on the ELMO, page 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically, I'd like to draw your attention to the passage towards the bottom of the page, which begins with the sentence: "During this incident it became clear to me that it was Kordic who was controlling the actions of the local police and the civilians." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is this, please? Where are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One inch up from the bottom of the second paragraph on the page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it here. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't have it. Page 3. Yes. Right. We have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were asked this question by Mr. Hayman in the Blaskic case on June the 3rd, 1998, at page 9142. The question was: "Is it also correct that during this incident it became clear to me that it was Kordic, it was Kordic who was controlling the actions of the local police and the civilians who were both blocking the roads and looting the convoy? Is that also true?" And your answer to that question, I believe, sir, was: "That is true, yes, but I would stress it was the local civilian police and not local military police. It's as it says in my transcript." Do you remember that exchange?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, you also went on to say that it was your view that in your -- in the Convoy of Joy incident, it was Mr. Kordic who commanded, if you like, the people, and it was Colonel Blaskic who commanded all of the HVO forces in that area, including the military police, or should; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, other than this single incident, are you aware of any other facts which established the existence or nature of Mr. Kordic's asserted control over the local police, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that for the Convoy of Joy, as we called it, when the word came to release the trucks and move them off, this was affected speedily, and both civilian and military police at that stage allowed things to happen within the hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the Convoy of Joy incident, any other facts, not opinions, that establish the existence or the nature of Mr. Kordic's asserted control over the local civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that he had assured me, I think on the -- we referred to it before on the 27th of September, when I took Colonel Williams to see him, that U.N. vehicles would have free access, freedom of routes. That involved those civilian police who were on roadblocks and military police. I mean, in order to let us go through, everyone who was manning roadblocks within the area would have to know that we were okay to go through. And he said that was going to happen. And he also denied us access to Stari Vitez, and that would involve preventing us getting through by some person or persons standing on a road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the sum total of the facts upon which you rely for that opinion that you articulated?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a fairly major commandability, if you like, to allow freedom of movement for a large area of all U.N. vehicles at his say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand it, you met Mr. Kordic on a grand total of five occasions, the first, I think you testified, on May the 9th?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two days before you formally took up your duties as commanding officer of the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And correct me if I'm wrong: The second incident, the second meeting, was on May the 19th? Yes?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I wouldn't contest that it's probably about five times that we met face to face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Just so that the record is clear, the third meeting was on June the 11th and the Convoy of Joy incident, as you described; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On September the 27th, about three or four months later, then you met Mr. Kordic in the Busovaca region; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, you had a farewell dinner with him on November the 6th?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 6th of October. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 6th of November?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask Mr. Kordic whether he had control over the military police or the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no particular reason to ask him. If I may, I could refer back to the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A very simple question, sir. It's a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer it.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite clear. I'd established a command system within that area where I relied specifically upon my liaison officers to give me information. And as a military man, my military focus in who I talked to was to Tihomir Blaskic as a military man. So we didn't have duplication. You will be aware also, I had a civil affairs officer, Mr. Randy Rhodes, and I was delighted to see him arrive, because he could deal with the civil matters, which he did, with the Mayor and Valenta and others. So the fact that I only saw Mr. Kordic -- yes, Mr. Kordic, on a number of occasions, is not unusual, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just wait for the interpreters. A point though, and I think you agreed with this: You never yourself ever asked him whether he had any control over either the civilian or the military police, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But, sir -- Your Honour, am I allowed to amplify slightly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never asked me if I had any control over my forces either. It's something -- it was taken for granted. He knew my position, I knew his position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask Colonel Blaskic whether Mr. Kordic had any control over the military police? You didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't ask anyone else in the HVO, either in the military or in the civilian government, did you, that particular question?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked no one -- I personally asked no one in the HVO. As I already testified, I had asked my officers, liaison officers, company commanders and patrols to find out the structure of the HVO and the command arrangements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Brigadier, I think we all understood that testimony. And I gather, from your opinion, then, that it's your view that the liaison officers charged with the task of conducting those inquiries would have been in the best position to make the determination of the control that Mr. Kordic had or did not have over the local police force; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were best placed within their areas to judge that, but I perhaps was the only person placed to judge the totality of what my ten liaison officers were doing. Now, I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the liaison officer most particularly charged with discovery of that information, I think, was Captain or then-Captain Lee Whitworth?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All my liaison officers were charged with that, because there were HVO police over the entire area, within the Vitez pocket, within Busovaca, down at Kiseljak, and certainly in Travnik within the early days. So it was a combined responsibility to find out what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn, if I may, to one other subject, the first meeting that you had on May the 9th of 1993 with Mr. Kordic. I believe that you had actually been taken by Colonel Stewart to see Colonel Blaskic on that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the first and only meeting that you had had with Colonel Blaskic in the presence of Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this was -- one of the purposes of this meeting was for me to be introduced to Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any notes or contemporaneous memoranda regarding this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that stage. I made some notes in my personal diary later on, when I reconstructed it, but at the time I was not, as it were, in the driving seat. It was a meeting that Colonel Stewart had arranged with Commander Blaskic. I was there because it was very early days, merely to get a feel for what was going on, to listen to the discussion, and to meet the various personalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any reference in a milinfosum to this conversation, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have at that stage been reading the milinfosums, I am sure; in fact, it would be unusual if it wasn't recorded in a milinfosum. But I couldn't recall the detail of the milinfosum. I know that we discussed primarily the matters surrounding Ahmici, as that was utmost in Colonel Stewart's mind at the moment, and I believed we had representatives from the ICRC there as well, and we discussed the problem of prisoners, which was a problem at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a clear memory of Colonel Blaskic explaining to you the three theories about which you've testified on direct examination, or is it only a vague recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a very clear memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it to you, sir, that actually you and Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart discussed, prior to going to this meeting, what Colonel Stewart was going to say, and just for the elucidation of the Prosecution, I am referring to the testimony of Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart in the Blaskic case in open session, pages 23810, 23811 and 23812. Let me put it to you, sir, that the decision was made to confront Colonel Blaskic and actually find out who was in command of the HVO forces, and indeed that's exactly what happened; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We conferred before the meeting, if you say conferred; we talked briefly about how to handle the meeting. And I've already described how Colonel Stewart was clearly going to take the lead and I would sit in the back seat. He was certainly going to ask some penetrating questions about Ahmici, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He actually stated to -- he challenged Colonel Tihomir Blaskic on the matter of who was in command, who was responsible for the soldiers of the HVO, and Colonel Blaskic actually confirmed before both of you that he was the Commander; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I mean, I don't have the benefit of this transcript, obviously, but that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it to you also, sir, that there was not actually any discussion of the three theories -- the Serbs, the Muslims themselves, or Muslims dressed as a HVO -- at that time; in fact, Colonel Blaskic never articulated that view to you. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that he did it, and he did it at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just read you a very brief exchange on page 23812 of Lieutenant-Colonel's testimony. He is being asked about page 310 of the book that he wrote, "Broken Lives," and this question is asked: "You recounted a meeting with Dario Kordic in which Mr. Kordic had suggested that the Serbs had been responsible for Ahmici? Do you recall that? Answer: I do. Question: I take it you find that an incredible explanation? Answer: Well, yes, I just -- I remember laughing myself sick. Question: Would you agree that Colonel Blaskic never made such an explanation to you for Ahmici? Answer: I would definitely agree that Colonel Blaskic never made such a statement to me, that the Serbs were responsible for that action, which, of course, goes to show you, you know, that Kordic was not a soldier."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, what you are putting, you know, is simply the evidence of another trial, of another witness. This witness can only give his own evidence. I'm not sure that we are really assisted. Colonel -- I'm sorry, Brigadier, does this make you change your mind in any way? I'm not sure of the point of the question.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've tried to relate the facts as I remember them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the fact that Bob Stewart's -- Colonel Bob Stewart has gone on the record and said that, I mean, I can't dispute that he said that. It is at odds with what I thought was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, why we are here is to hear your evidence, not to hear what somebody else said about it. And Mr. Sayers, if you want to challenge the evidence in this way, putting it to this witness, of course, doesn't do that. You'll have to call the witness. Now, I don't think we are going to get much further with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I am inclined to agree, Mr. President. I don't think we will, in view of the witness's testimony. But let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the briefing that you received from Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart regarding the situation, the political and military situation, isn't it true that Colonel Stewart told you that Colonel Blaskic was, in his opinion, the real commander of the HVO in Central Bosnia, that he never thought that Kordic was the commander and never referred to Kordic as the commander or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart briefed me on the orbat, similar to the one we discussed. He certainly mentioned that Blaskic was the op zone commander, the commander of the HVO in the area, but I believe he was talking about the HVO military and that he was the military man responsible for the Vitez area. I'm aware that the HVO is more than military, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it also true that he instructed you that whenever Colonel Blaskic said something, it happened lower down, and that he, therefore, felt that it was reasonable to assume that Colonel Blaskic had effective command and control over his forces in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very reasonable to assume. I can't imagine that Colonel Stewart would have gone on talking to Blaskic throughout his entire time, and certainly I would have not talked to Blaskic in my time if I thought that he didn't have an influence and effect and an efficient command train, which he had, and that is witnessed by the excellent defence by the Bosnian Croat forces of that Vitez pocket. You would have to have a very efficient, well-organised command chain to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Colonel Stewart had actually never met Mr. Anto Valenta before the day that you and he went to go to see this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's true, yes. I think he mentioned to me that -- he commented it was unusual when Valenta had asked me to go up see him on, I think, the 12th, if my memory serves me right, because he had never seen Valenta himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a few preliminary questions relating to the May the 19th meeting in Busovaca. This was the second meeting that you'd had with Mr. Kordic, and I believe that you had been invited by him to lunch, together with a gathering of local politicians and soldiers, as well as you and Lieutenant-Colonel Schipper; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was on this occasion that you invented the name for the mountain lodge as the Eagle's Nest, I think was your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's also correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you made that choice of name deliberately and consciously, did you not, for the images that it evoked?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that eight days into your tour, you had branded the Croats as Nazis; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wouldn't be correct. Eight days into my tour, I had been part of and witnessed the shovelling of charred bodies into plastic bags; I had seen scenes of destructions, people being killed; I had heard from the milinfosums what was going on. With that background, and with a very vicious war going on, where, I would admit, atrocities appeared to be committed by both sides, when you are then taken for lunch to a hunting lodge in a wooded area, a mountainous wooded area of one of the most beautiful parts of that country, there was a stark flashback in my mind, and I'm sorry if that's a product of my education and my upbringing, but I made this juxtaposition. It was a reaction. I'm not making an excuse for that reaction, but I'm saying that it was my honest reaction at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to Exhibit Z2653, which was the orbat you were shown, or one of the orbats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder whether the usher would get a copy of Z2535,1, which is an earlier version of this orbat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think it is in those package of materials that you have in front of you. It was earlier admitted. It's Z2535,1. Taking a look at Exhibit Z2535,1, Brigadier, this was an orbat, or an order of battle, prepared by your military information officer, Captain Simon Harrison; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it shows the operations zone for Central Bosnia, Vitez/Travnik, reporting to the HVO command in Mostar, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's at the top of the page. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the general staff to whom Colonel Blaskic reported, sir? That was General Milivoj Petkovic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Petkovic, yes, whom I'd met on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the offices of the general staff of the HVO were actually located in Mostar, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are not suggesting, sir, that the dotted line that connects the political wing, HDZ, and the -- well, we'll confine our attention to that for the time being. You're not suggesting that that dotted line indicates any kind of a command relationship with the HVO military forces, or that the HVO was under the command of the HDZ/BiH, are you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am. That dotted line implies entirely that there is a relationship between the two. The dotted line is, as it says, the political wing of the HDZ and the op zone, and the reason for that is because -- well, firstly, their offices were in the same building, in Vitez town, and we believed that there was unusual political direction on the operations of the HVO forces. I think you'll note, and if my memory serves me right, if you looked at the similar level of command in the BiH army, we did not show a similar political structure in that place because we did not believe there was the same relationship between the politics and the military in the BiH as there was in the HVO. There was a different relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember being asked to explain the significance of that dotted line one and a half years ago in the Blaskic case, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall my exact words. You probably have them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Page 9045 to 9046 of the Blaskic transcript. The question was for you to explain the significance of the line, "... the one without the Xs first ..." in other words, the dotted line, and your answer was as follows: A Sir, if I might briefly explain this. This was prepared by my military information officer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. The interpreters do not have that text. A -- Captain Simon Harrison, and it shows on the top line, in the centre, the op zone Central Bosnia, Vitez/Travnik, with a commander, Tihomir Blaskic, and a deputy commander, Franjo Nakic. On the left of that, with a dotted line, because it is not under command or in a command relationship, is the political wing of the HDZ. Do you remember giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what you're reading from my testimony, then that is probably what I said, yes. I would have to obviously admit that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Brigadier, may I ask you, then, what is your evidence today as to the significance of, first, the broken line between the political wing and the op zone and any other unbroken line? What is the significance of the difference between those two?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. The unbroken line is what we'd call direct command and, therefore, there is a clear command chain. That is a solid line, the clear command chain. The broken line is a relationship between the two headquarters, which may run from liaison to the exchange of information to the exchange of policy, or whatever, but it doesn't imply that one has primacy over the other, particularly as they are put there on the same line, the top line, sir. So we thought, and I had them inserted for equal status but on that same line. And as it shows on the right of that diagram, similarly, that dotted line across again to the joint commission in Travnik, which was a BiH-HVO joint command of equal status but not under command. Does that make it clear, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I gather you're saying, then, the broken line does signify some relationship.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Yes, sir. It is a relationship of liaison, of exchange of policies and ideas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just go into some background matters, General, and I'll try to move through these fairly quickly. You were in command of the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire in Central Bosnia from May the 11th, 1993 to November the 12th, 1993; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your mission was to facilitate the supply of humanitarian aid through Central Bosnia, up as far as Tuzla in northern Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mission was to ensure the delivery of aid into and throughout my area of responsibility, yes. In broad terms, the very thing you've said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this involved giving armed protection to UNHCR or U.N.-sponsored organisations; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself, sir, do not speak Croatian, I take it.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak a few words of greetings and familiarities, but that is it, sir. Could I just add that was a deliberate policy, not to speak Croatian, in order to avoid misunderstandings, which I've seen before with interpreters -- or without interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The liaison officer for Busovaca, I believe, was Captain Boris Cowan; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Bruce Cowan but he was known as Boris.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, did you make any personal notes in your diary connected with your conversation with Mr. Valenta in early May of 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use those notes to refresh your recollection before you came to testify about that conversation yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if we might make to an application to see any notes that the Brigadier has consulted to refresh his recollection, obviously with any personal information excised and redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution seen these notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you have any objection to showing the parties your notes?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I do, for a number of reasons; first, because I had been going through a very messy divorce with my wife, there were a lot of very personal notes in my diaries and in my notebooks, not only to do with that, but to do with a lot of other matters, to do with the reports and performance of my soldiers, how I felt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt for a moment. Clearly, those personal matters would not be discloseable. But I suppose one way to deal with it would be for you to black out all the -- to get a copy, if this wouldn't be too much trouble, and highlight out all the personal bits and just produce the bits relating to conversations with Valenta and the like. Is that a possible solution?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that's technically possible, yes, sir. I mean, if I can be entirely honest, sir, I'm somewhat unhappy because, in my mind, that would create a precedent to opening up the rest of my diary, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it shouldn't. It's merely a solution which we sometimes employ to get around the difficulty. You would have control of your diary. You would simply produce, when you come next, the extracts which relate to your evidence, I mean, if that is, first of all, a practicable solution and, second of all, one which isn't going to involve you in too much administrative work.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any objection to that, Mr. Sayers? You only want the bit about, say, the conversation about Valenta?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The ones that we're particularly concerned with are conversations with, obviously, our client, Mr. Kordic, if there are any entries in the diary that relate to that.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. The entries in my notebooks, had I realised I'd be sitting in a court now, would have been made much neater at the time. I have a problem reading my own writing at times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It applies to a number of us. Would you do that? Now, if, for any reason, you change your mind or you get into difficulty, you find it difficult, or whatever, then would you be in touch with the Prosecution about that, you'll have leave to talk to them, so that they may know, if necessary, and an application can be made to the Court or matters can be resolved in one way or another. But, otherwise, would you come with those redacted or, as we call it here, edited highlights from your diary?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. I mean, obviously, we need to establish now, in order that I don't miss any bits out, exactly what is required between now and the 25th. I am entirely willing to comply with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suspect any conversations that you've had that you've related in your evidence or any of the incidents which you've related in your evidence. So it's those things which you've covered.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, sir, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any notes relating to those, but cutting out any personal matters and comments about your soldiers or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, you could assist, no doubt. If the witness is in difficulty for any reason, of course, he can tell you and you can either bring the matter up with the Court or discuss it with the Defence to find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. This is the first time that this problem arises before this Chamber. A solution has been suggested, and we shall do whatever we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, did you ever have the occasion to see Mr. Kordic on press conferences during the seven months that you spent in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to scrutinise any translations of materials that he had apparently authored?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But could I just add that for the majority of the time I would expect that to have been done by my civil affairs officer, Mr. Randy Rhodes. And if there had been anything of importance that Mr. Rhodes thought that I should see, then he would have made sure I'd seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, though, Brigadier, that sitting here today you don't remember any such materials?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The views that were expressed to you by Mr. Valenta that you found distasteful, isn't it a fact that Mr. Kordic didn't express any analogous views to you during the five meetings that had you with him?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct and quite correct. But, I mean, I have to remember they are working for the same organisations. They are going to the same political meetings, as we've already discussed. They were sent down south. They were in the -- his office; I believe he had an office in Hotel Vitez, which Mr. Valenta also used. I must admit I never went to that office, but they were working together. Could I just add that, I mean, if Mr. Valenta did not want me to know those views, he clearly wouldn't have got hold of me three days into my operational tour and briefed me quite clearly on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valenta had only recently arrived in Vitez, had he not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I have to take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's true that Mr. Kordic never articulated any views to you that would suggest that he subscribed to these extremist theories that were voiced to you by Mr. Valenta; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one general question, sir, and I think that you've actually written a paper on this particular subject. But in wartime, would you not agree that it's perfectly normal for the warring forces to try to use the press to -- and media to build up an image of their own status, the power and strength of their forces and, correspondingly, the weakness of the opponent forces? That's fairly standard in wartime, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's fairly standard. It has to be handled with great care, as I explained in my article. Otherwise you can do more damage to your own side. Perhaps I should add that the only other article I have written for the military is on military ethics, which is about behaviours and standards in warfare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in terms of the use of the press to build up your own impression of your own power, exaggeration and hyperbole are part of the verbal arsenal, if you like, of the press forces of warring factions, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are using exaggeration and hyperbole on what is a basic truth, yes. If you are using exaggeration and hyperbole on what is untrue, then you are using a very dangerous tactic that can backfire on you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself, sir, I think in your extensive and impressive military background, have received considerable training in the Geneva Conventions and their applications and also in the other instruments of International Humanitarian Law; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although not as much, perhaps, as I'd like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of training programme was in place for the HVO troops regarding the Geneva Conventions or matters relating to International Humanitarian Law?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not specifically know that, but I would surmise that anyone who is a signatory to that and ratified the Geneva Conventions would be bound to produce training programmes to give their soldiers a minimum knowledge of military law, and the law of armed conflict as it applies to soldiers fighting both in internal conflict and, if you like, in more general external war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But you simply do not know whether any such of a regime was in place for the HVO forces, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, no. I mean, in a well-disciplined and well-organised force, which the HVO was, there was training done, and I was very much aware that soldiers were trained. That force has also published a set of rules and regulations, as we are also aware. I would be surprised if for their protection they had not done such training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two areas that you covered, which I will address extremely briefly, the first relating to complaints of ethnic cleansing on both sides. There is no question that your office received regular complaints from the HVO and also from the other side, the Muslim side, concerning alleged forcible expulsion of civilians from their homes throughout your tour; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similarly, constant complaints were made by both sides about their civilian detainees being used to dig trenches and for other kinds of manual labour? That's true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself, however, in all of your seven months in the area, never actually saw any civilians being used to dig trenches, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But, as I've tried to point out before, my journeys were quick and fast to talk to the right level of commander. If anyone would have seen it, it would be my liaison officers or my soldiers on patrol in the ground. It would be, I would have thought, highly unlikely that I would have seen any anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it the same goes for prisoners of war, soldiers being used for the same functions; you never actually saw any soldiers being impressed into trench-digging operations or other items of manual labour, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't -- I'm somewhat confused as to why you are asking these questions, because, I mean, it's obvious I have not seen them, but others would have done perhaps. Because I haven't seen them, doesn't mean I didn't believe they were happening. And the reports came in from both sides to say they were happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me address with you -- you gave some brief testimony concerning the Vance-Owen Plan, I believe. Were you familiar with the way that that plan was actually intended to operate, or the provisions of it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's a huge plan. I am familiar that it was a -- one of the attempts at bringing a political and peaceful solution to the area, by suggesting a partition into various areas for the three warring factions at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That level of detail I am aware of. Below that, apart from being aware on occasions as various versions came out as to where lines were being drawn, I was aware of that. Our information as to the detail of that plan relied on some very poor faxes, where some of the lines could have been a couple of kilometres wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Suffice it to say that in connection with the actual map-drawing exercise that was part of the Vance-Owen Plan, there was considerable disagreement with the contours of those lines on the part of the ABiH forces in Travnik, for example; was there not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, to be honest. I thought I had enough to do trying to get the aid through than worrying about somebody else's job. Whilst I welcomed a political solution, I wasn't going to get involved. Again it goes back -- this was not my place to talk to the politicians about these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Did you have any understanding about the way that the political organisation of these proposed cantons was supposed to work, or was that something that you did not pay a great deal of attention to?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of cantons, and I was also aware of, if you like, the ethnic balance that would have come out of some of those cantons, and therefore the hope that the political organisation set up would reflect those ethnic minorities or majorities, but not in great detail, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware in province 10, for example, the Travnicka province -- and just for the Court's information, I am referring to Exhibit S571,1, which was the Vance-Owen Plan, put into evidence by the Prosecution. There is an annex that explains how the political organisation of each of these provinces was supposed to work at page 138 and 139. Were you aware, sir, that the provincial governor of province 10 was destined to be chosen by the Croat political party?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. And, as I've said, in my position of hopefully impartiality, it would have been wrong of me to make any comments which might prejudice the outcome of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe we can truncate this line of questioning. Would it be fair to say, and I think you have said this, that you don't really know about the political organisation; the fact that the vice-governor was going to be appointed by the Muslim political party; that there was going to be a provincial interim government of 10, with five members selected by the Muslim political party, four by the Croat political party, and one by the Serbs? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, but I knew in principle that there would be some sort of power-sharing arrangement. The exact detail I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware that Kiseljak and the so-called Kiseljak or River Lepenica Valley was not in province 10, the so-called Croat-controlled province?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I can't, in all honesty, say I was aware of that. I mean, I was aware of the structure but, as I say, I really didn't get involved in speculative plans, because my pouring over the Vance-Owen Plan and trying to decipher it would not have helped my job in that pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's depart from that subject and just step back to the historical context of your seven-month tour. It would be fair to say that from May of 1993 onwards, the Croat military forces in Central Bosnia suffered a series of serious military defeats at the hands of advancing Muslim forces? That's true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was, if you like, a situation of stalemate with some Croat initiatives just before I arrived. There then was a major offensive by the BiH, and that then stabilised to leave the pocket situation. And that is where I left the situation, with a stable pocket situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that there were, I think in Central Bosnia, four isolated enclaves when you arrived? The first would be the Vitez-Busovaca pocket, the second the Kiseljak pocket, the third the Vares pocket, the fourth the Zepce pocket; and actually, there is a fifth one, the Kakanj area. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they would be classed as pockets when I arrived. They certainly hardened into pockets later on. I can't speak about Zepce, Kakanj or Vares in any detail. It was my impression, when I first arrived, that there was a degree of movement of individuals still going on between the areas that later polarised as pockets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
