utterances.text: If I could ask you to look at the revised orbat about which you testified, Exhibit Z2,653. Put that on the ELMO for everybody's reference. A number of these brigades, sir, have crosses through them. Those are brigades that were eliminated as the result of military defeats suffered by the Croat forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. If I could explain, the normal form on amendments to these documents would be initially a deletion of those units that had disappeared to all intents and purposes, followed by a reissue at a later date of an amended version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Frankopan brigade and the Travnicka brigade ceased to exist as a result of a major Muslim offensive between June the 8th and the June the 12th in Travnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot challenge the dates, but if you are referring to -- I think it's the Francopan and the Travnicka. Yes, they were destroyed to all intents and purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similarly, the Jure Francetic Brigade had been destroyed in Zenica, I believe, prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that would have been prior to my arrival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going over to the right, the Kotromanic brigade had been destroyed as a result of Croat military defeats in Kakanj in June of 1993, pretty much simultaneously with the defeats suffered by the Croats in Travnik? Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, these details are as in the footnotes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to round out this line of questioning, Brigadier, the Bobovac brigade in Vares was destroyed as a result of the capture of Vares in the first part of November of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Destroyed, I think, is perhaps -- would be better to say defeated, in that most of the people who could get away, obviously, re-formed into other organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, when you leave this topic, it would be about time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I was just about to enter into another topic, Mr. President, so this would be a fine time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. And do you anticipate we should be able to finish on the morning of the 25th? Perhaps you would like to think about that and try and concentrate on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will, as always, and I hope the Trial Chamber has seen that we have been making efforts to do this. We will try to do so, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Brigadier, if you'd be back, please, on the morning of the 25th. If you could provide a photocopy of your notes, as I say, with the relevant bits blacked out. If, in any way, providing it is onerous or proves impossible, perhaps you could get in touch with the Prosecution about it and let them know. If, on the other hand, you are able to do it without too much difficulty, if you could let us have it earlier, so people can read it before the hearing. And that will save time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to go now, please, and be back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Kovacic was first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to say that I would also probably have quite a few questions. It depends how much Mr. Sayers will take from me, but I certainly will have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have in mind that you said earlier that you would. I haven't forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just take this opportunity to explain to the Tribunal -- it will only take a minute or so -- that we have filed today, but have copies available here in Court, the document that I forecast was coming this week about witnesses and our present position on witnesses who remain to be called. The document is available. I hope it's with -- it's not available. Yes. Here they come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall take it as unfiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These have been filed confidentially, and so they will be available to my learned friends in due course. The format of the document may be worth just a minute's explanation while it's being distributed. If the Chamber goes immediately to page 13, it will see something begins "Witnesses by Category." Now, what follows from page 13 is, essentially, what you have between pages 3 and 12 but differently ordered. So the document comes with two different ways of presenting information, for your assistance. I am asked whether we should be in private session. I don't think we need be in private session, although there is one thing that I am going to mention that is a touch delicate. If the Chamber then comes back to the beginning, to page 2, this sets out with some notes our present position. It's not an invitation to intervention in any way with our list or an acceptance that it requires intervention; it's an expression of our current position. And if the Chamber then goes to page 3, it will find a table which reflects the overview of witnesses, which I trust the Chamber found helpful. And so what happens there is we've identified, according to codes that are explained, the various witnesses whose evidence should be before you. Now, I am revealing in this document those for whom we are seeking subpoenas. Applications for subpoenas have been lodged ex parte and confidential in the usual way, but of course the Defence will now know from this document, because it seemed helpful for everyone to know, which witnesses we now judge we are going to be dealing with by subpoena. But they will recognise that that knowledge is something they should not impart elsewhere. It should remain confidential. But if, without putting a name on it, you look at the bottom of page 3, the very first witness, you'll see that witness is a witness, T.B.C., to be called in respect of whom a subpoena may be required. If we go to page 4 of this document, you'll see, in the second column, that for your convenience I'm simply following through the original overview of witness page numbers, so the next witness can be found at page 6 of the original overview. He's not to be called because a transcript will suffice, N.T.B.C.T. The next witness, again, I won't put a name, features at page 7 of the overview and is a witness to be called, willing to attend. So, in that way, the first part of this document, going from page 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and through to 8, deals with all those first witnesses. The first category of witnesses in the overview says which ones should be before you and the method by which they should be before you, whether by being called, by being a transcript of evidence from another case, by being in affidavit form, or otherwise, and the notes on the right-hand side explain the position. From page 8, not surprisingly, we pick it up with international witnesses, that goes through to page 9, 10; then at 11, international armed conflict witnesses; at 12, experts and the improper term, quasi-experts, has crept in there, but we can overlook that, experts; then there is a residual list of to-be-decided witnesses, with comments beside them. When you come to page 13, that same information has been rescheduled according to categories, so that starting at page 13, these are the witnesses to be called who are willing, and they are listed on the following pages. If you go to page 17, at the foot of 17, you'll see the list of those in respect of whom a subpoena is required; 18, witnesses whose evidence can be dealt with by affidavit or statement; at 21, witnesses by transcript. So that the same information appears, scheduled in two different ways for your convenience. You'll discover that the village crime base witnesses are not dealt with in this list. They're explained at the beginning, an explanation I've given before; namely, that you will be presented with village binders, which are further explained in this document, and then, having considered the state of evidence about the village and whether witnesses who we propose should be before you can be agreed or read, or whether they have to be called, then the village crime base witnesses may be additional. The position, subject to the village crime base witnesses, is that, starting today and including the present witness, I think there are 39 witnesses identified; that should leave 26 witnesses after Christmas, of whom 13 should be very short. That's the position, and I hope it's an informative document and helps the Chamber in the way that it wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other point, while I'm on my feet, and I can say that perhaps Mr. Lopez-Terres would find it a little more difficult, there is a concern about some inconsistency in relation to the approach to diaries, I know. It doesn't concern us because we quite understand the need for particular witnesses to produce whatever material they're happy to produce, but based on the previous practice, for example, with General Cordy-Simpson, I think the announced policy was that wherever a witness looks at a document but doesn't show it to us and doesn't want it to be produced, but refreshes his memory from it, then it probably won't be produced. I repeat: We're not concerned, save to say that we must be able to tell witnesses what the position is if they inquire. It seems to me that this witness was, in the event, content, at the questioning of the Court, to make available extracts from his diary, but I gently remind the Court that there may be something of an inconsistency, and we've got to be careful how we approach our witnesses on these delicate issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, when do you think -- I don't know if you can answer me today -- but when do you believe you will be able to conclude the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That question can be answered, of course, by knowledge of how long each witness will take and what court sittings are available, knowing the problems that the Tribunal has with other commitments. If I'm right, there are about 26 witnesses after Christmas, plus maybe a few village witnesses, and if 13 of those are very short witnesses who can be dealt with many per day, and 13 are reasonable length witnesses, then my guess, without checking with Ms. Verhaag on statistics, is that recently we've been dealing with substantial witnesses at something between one and two sessions per witness. It started off rather longer; it was about two sessions for a substantial witness, sometimes longer. We've now got it down to one, sometimes a little bit more. So if there are 13 substantial witnesses, that might be, say, 20 sessions, and if there are 13 short witnesses, then it will be a few more session than that. It's more realistic to think in terms of sessions, particularly given the uncertainties that there are about the scheduling of the Court's diaries for reasons outside of our control. Maybe these matters can be more helpfully dealt with, so far as timetable is concerned, at a Status Conference, now that the information is available to you.
